text: In October 1933 a camp opened in a former sugar mill building at Holstendorf, near Ahrensbök, to take pressure off overcrowded custody sites in Eutin and Bad Schwartau. Johann Heinrich Böhmcker set it up to hold a few dozen prisoners for road work; in December 1933 the prisoners were moved to an old shoe factory in Ahrensbök.

Until the camp closed in May 1934, at least 94 people were held at Ahrensbök, most of them Communists, along with Social Democrats, conservative opponents, and even rivals of Böhmcker inside his own party.

The Ahrensbök camp grew out of Böhmcker's personal initiative: it gave work to SA men he made auxiliary police, and he used it to pressure wealthy opponents, until the Oldenburg Gestapo reprimanded him. He also wrote his own rules so prisoners could be used for labor.
Böhmcker picked Holstendorf so prisoners could finish an unfinished Labor Service road project. Unlike most early camps, Ahrensbök worked like a forced labor camp, and the Reich paid for the work.

Treasury records show Reich payments for the camp, and camp commandant Theodor Christian Tenhaaf's postmark appears on the paperwork. The Lübeck district, where Böhmcker had held power since 1932, became an early testing ground for persecution; at least 345 residents were taken into custody within a year.
No prisoners died at Ahrensbök, but there was mistreatment. After the war, Tenhaaf and some guards were tried in Lübeck, and Tenhaaf received a prison sentence of three and a half years.
The Hannover police opened a camp inside the Moringen workhouse in April 1933, with Müller as its first commandant. The institution had long served as an orphanage, prison, and workhouse.
In March 1933, Gottschick of Hannover asked workhouse director Hugo Krack about housing a 200-prisoner camp at Moringen. Krack moved the infirmary to make room and set a daily charge per detainee.

The men's camp held about 321 detainees a month, but most were released within weeks, according to medical files studied by Hans Hesse. Most were Communists; Hermann Wenskowski recalled the first Jehovah's Witness arriving at Moringen in June 1933.

Müller arrived with about 50 Hannover police officers plus local SA, SS, and Stahlhelm deputies. He and Krack wrote house rules based on reeducation, and Krack clashed with each commandant over who was in charge.
Prisoners were encouraged to attend chapel services. Attendance rose quickly, and Müller later found that prisoners were using the chapel for secret political meetings.
On May 1, 1933, the detainees were put on display and made to listen to Nazi radio, and a local paper praised Moringen's discipline. By the end of May, 300 detainees had been released.
In June 1933, Stockhofe became the new commandant, and the first women detainees arrived at Moringen.

After guards silenced prisoners singing Communist songs, 28 prisoners began a hunger strike at Moringen, organized by August Baumgarte, Johannes Engelke, Kurt Fröse, August Steffens, August Tünnermann, and Viktor Zudrowitz. Stockhofe blamed newly arrived detainees from Osnabrück.

To break the strike, Krack isolated the strikers and ordered their water cut off, despite early objections from Stockhofe and the physician Otto Wolten-Pecksen. Krack told Bergin of the Hannover police he did not care about the consequences. Baumgarte later described the thirst. The strike ended after a few days with a promise of better food.
As punishment for the strike, the police sharply limited prisoners' mail and parcels.

In August 1933, Otto Cordes of the SS took command of Moringen, following Heinrich Himmler's takeover of police authority. Krack had already asked Bergin to replace the police guards with SS men. Few detainees had work.

Friedrich Flohr became the last commandant in September and imposed a harsher regime at Moringen. Prisoners were beaten and tortured; Otto Bokelmann died from torture, and August Witte died of injuries from an earlier police prison. Krack complained about the SS violence.
In the fall of 1933, Moringen was turned into a women's camp. Men were sent to Papenburg in exchange for women, and the remaining men went to Oranienburg. Krack ran the women's camp until 1938.
Cordes died in 1944. In 1948, a Göttingen court sentenced Flohr for crimes against humanity, and Krack and Wolter-Pecksen testified against him.
